clue.text: Characters ultimately help Boycie deliver motors to Nelson Mandela House

indicators.note: ultimately says to take the final letter of each of the words that follow, help through House

parts.words: help Boycie deliver motors to Nelson Mandela House

explanation.surface: A dodgy car dealer from Only Fools and Horses delivers vehicles to the Trotters' tower block.
explanation.walkthrough: Boycie is a used-car dealer in the sitcom Only Fools and Horses, and Nelson Mandela House is the Peckham tower block where the Trotters live.
explanation.definitionFit: Personae are the roles or figures in a play or story, as in dramatis personae.

clue.text: Cassandra's somewhat stuck-up habits — I miss episode

indicators.note: stuck-up says the hidden letters are read backwards
somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone haughty confesses to missing an episode of a favourite show, perhaps Rodney's wife Cassandra.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'stuck-up' means read upwards. The definition reads 'Cassandra is', the 's standing for 'is'; Cassandra is also Rodney's wife in Only Fools and Horses.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassandra, the Trojan prophetess doomed to foretell disaster unheeded, is a byword for a doom-monger.

clue.text: Marlene's fancy for macho types

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or reworked, so the name's letters are rearranged

parts.note: Marlene is Boycie's wife in Only Fools and Horses; the 's links fodder and indicator

explanation.surface: Boycie's wife Marlene has a taste for rugged, manly men.
explanation.definitionFit: Real men is a jokey idiom for tough, traditionally masculine males, the macho sort.

clue.text: Diversion — reversed on Hooky Street

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: something turned outside in, i.e. inside out, has been reversed

indicators.note: hooky is slang for crooked or stolen, so the letters of the word Street are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: A pastime, flipped over on a street of dodgy deals, recalling Del Boy's Hooky Street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooky Street' looks like a place (Del Boy's dream destination of easy money), but 'Hooky' is the anagram signal and Street is shuffled to TEREST.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobby or sideline pursued away from one's main work is an outside interest, a diversion.

clue.text: Idiot to help with bird stuffing

indicators.note: stuffing says the bird is packed inside the word for help

parts.note: to aid is to help
the rhea is a large flightless South American bird

explanation.surface: A fool tries to help with stuffing a bird, perhaps the Christmas turkey.
explanation.definitionFit: An airhead is slang for a foolish, empty-headed person.

clue.text: Peckham's outsiders drinking highball on vacation, say it's cool

indicators.note: drinking says the outer letters swallow what follows
outsiders means just the first and last letters of the place name

parts.note: Peckham is the south London district where Only Fools and Horses is set

indicators.note: a word on vacation has been emptied, leaving only its outer letters

parts.note: say is EG, for example

explanation.surface: In a Peckham pub, someone downs an empty highball glass and declares it cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's' is a link: the wordplay is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Phlegm in its old sense is calm composure, the unflappable coolness of the phlegmatic.

clue.text: Polishing crystal chandelier is hard occasionally — with bulky ladders initially misplaced — if they go wrong: crash!

indicators.note: polishing works something over, so the gathered letters are rubbed into a new order
occasionally means taking every other letter of the phrase crystal chandelier is hard
misplaced means a letter has gone missing from the word bulky
initially picks the opening letter of ladders, the letter that is lost

explanation.surface: A recollection of the Only Fools and Horses scene where the Trotters polish a chandelier and it crashes down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'occasionally' gives RSACADLEIHR from the even letters; 'misplaced' drops L ('ladders initially') from BULKY to leave BUKY; 'Polishing' shuffles the lot. In the episode the chandelier crashes to the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: Hydraulic brakes are a vehicle's fluid-operated stopping system, so their failure means a collision.

clue.text: Celebrity cycling over our entrance

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits over the second
cycling moves the end letter of the word round to the front

parts.note: a celebrity is a big name

explanation.surface: A famous person rides a bike over the threshold of our house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrance' is not a doorway but the verb en-TRANCE, to charm.
explanation.definitionFit: To enamour someone is to captivate or charm them, as to entrance does.

clue.text: Mike has no cap on very cold tooth

parts.note: Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet; also the barman of the Nag's Head

indicators.note: having no cap means the first letter is removed

parts.note: polar means very cold

explanation.surface: Mike, without a hat, has a tooth that is aching in the freezing weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A molar is one of the grinding teeth at the back of the mouth.

clue.text: Trigger gets on the radio show highlights

parts.note: to trigger something is to start it; Trigger is also the dim road-sweeper in Only Fools and Horses

indicators.note: on the radio says the word is heard, not seen

parts.note: to get money is to earn it

explanation.surface: Trigger, the Only Fools and Horses road sweeper, gets a spot on radio show highlights.
explanation.definitionFit: Star turns are the main acts on a bill, the best bits of a show.

clue.text: Consequently, Damien's under bar bearing drink

indicators.note: in a down clue this piece sits under the first

parts.note: so means consequently

indicators.note: bar means except, so the word for bearing is taken out

parts.note: Damien is Del Boy's son in Only Fools and Horses
mien is a person's bearing or manner

explanation.surface: Damien ends up under a bar, carrying a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Soda is a fizzy soft drink or mixer.

clue.text: Figure without a jack-of-all-trades

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the doll goes round the a

parts.note: a doll is a small figure

explanation.surface: Someone lacking a good figure is a general handyman.
explanation.definitionFit: A do-all is a factotum who handles every sort of task.

clue.text: Feet and inches are measurements British insist on using first of all

indicators.note: first of all says to take the opening letter of each of the words inches to insist

explanation.surface: A Briton insists that feet and inches be the units used first of all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feet' looks like a length beside inches, but it means metrical feet in verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Iambi, plural of iambus, are poetic metrical units of a short syllable then a long.

clue.text: Take pains as consequence and regret eating eggs on the counter

parts.note: an end is an outcome or consequence

indicators.note: counter as running against, so the combined letters are turned backwards
eating says the eggs go inside the word for regret

parts.note: to rue is to regret
ova are eggs

explanation.surface: A café worker regrets eating the eggs left out on the counter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the counter' looks like the café worktop, but counter means running against, so the regret-and-eggs piece is read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To endeavour is to try hard, to make a real effort.

clue.text: Insinuation affected nurse following house party

indicators.note: the following pieces come after the house

parts.note: an inn is a public house
U stands for upper-class, the manner an affected speaker puts on
EN is an enrolled nurse
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A nurse with put-on airs turns up after a house party, hinting at goings-on.
explanation.definitionFit: Innuendo is an indirect remark hinting at something, often suggestive.

clue.text: Priest detailed what may be thrown at wedding after Raquel's back in church

indicators.note: the trimmed confetti comes after the church piece
in says the letter goes inside the church

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: back means the last letter of the name

parts.note: Raquel is Del Boy's partner in Only Fools and Horses

indicators.note: detailed means its tail, the final letter, is cut off

parts.words: what may be thrown at wedding
parts.note: rice is traditionally thrown over newlyweds

explanation.surface: A priest describes what guests throw at a wedding after Raquel returns to the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'detailed' looks like 'described', but it means de-tailed: RICE loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleric is a member of the clergy, such as a priest.

clue.text: Pack Reliant Robin, say and supply any rug

parts.note: the Reliant Robin is a British three-wheeled car, an example of a car; the Trotters drive a Reliant Regal van

indicators.note: supply read as supple-ly, bendily, so the letters of any rug are bent into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone packs their Reliant Robin and supplies a rug for the journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supply' looks like the verb to provide but is read as an adverb from supple, the anagram signal. 'Pack' is slang for being armed, as in packing heat.
explanation.definitionFit: To pack, in criminal slang, is to be armed with a firearm.

clue.text: Content to leave The Nag's Head with a half-pint — landlord has one

indicators.note: with the content gone only the outer letters of the word remain
head means the first letter
half means the back half of the word's letters

explanation.surface: A drinker is happy to leave the Nag's Head, the Trotters' local pub, with half a pint the landlord kept.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nag's Head is the Trotters' local in Only Fools and Horses. 'half' takes NT, the second half of PINT.
explanation.definitionFit: A landlord lets property to a tenant, the person who rents it.

clue.text: Eccentric Uncle Albert's big character's right for this sort of family

indicators.note: eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters of uncle are rearranged
the big character is the capital letter that begins the name

parts.note: Uncle Albert is the old seafaring uncle in Only Fools and Horses

explanation.surface: Uncle Albert's larger-than-life personality is just right for this kind of family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'big character' looks like describing Albert's personality but means his capital A.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuclear family is the household unit of parents and their children alone.

clue.text: Reason for copper to bring up a free solicitor

parts.note: a pro is a reason in favour, as in pros and cons
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

indicators.note: free of a, so the a is taken out

parts.note: to rear a child is to bring it up

explanation.surface: A police officer explains why he arrested a freed lawyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'solicitor' is not a lawyer here but someone who solicits on behalf of others, a pimp.
explanation.definitionFit: A procurer obtains sexual partners for clients, soliciting for them, so is a pimp.

clue.text: Inexperienced lawyer volunteers unvarnished facts

parts.note: raw means green or inexperienced
a DA is a district attorney
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: A green lawyer offers some plain facts to the court.
explanation.definitionFit: Raw data is information as collected, before any processing or interpretation.

clue.text: After sign of neglect, in retirement, Del took stock

indicators.note: the reversed name comes after the rust

parts.note: rust forms on metal that has been neglected

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the name is read backwards

explanation.surface: Del Boy, having retired, does a stocktake after noticing signs of neglect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'took stock' looks like checking inventory but means stole livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: To rustle is to steal cattle or other livestock.

clue.text: Painful condition overwhelming international winger?

indicators.note: overwhelming says the condition engulfs the letter

parts.note: IBS is irritable bowel syndrome

explanation.surface: An international wide player is laid low by a painful complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'winger' wants to be a footballer, but the question mark flags a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibis is a long-billed wading bird, something with wings.

clue.text: In retrospect police unit say Del Boy's brief was originally an accessory

indicators.note: looking back means the letters are read backwards

parts.note: the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department
Del (delete) is an example of a key on a keyboard

indicators.note: brief means cut short, losing the last letter

parts.note: Boy as in Del Boy

indicators.note: originally means the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Looking back, a police team says Del Boy's lawyer was originally an accomplice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Del Boy' reads as one name, but Del is a computer key and Boy is shortened. 'accessory' looks criminal but is a clothing item.
explanation.definitionFit: A dickey bow is a bow tie, an item worn to finish an outfit.

clue.text: After doubling his final instalment, Del has gold furnishings

indicators.note: his last letter, a Roman fifty, is doubled to a Roman hundred

parts.note: Del Boy of Only Fools and Horses
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: Del, having doubled his last payment, now owns gold fittings.
explanation.walkthrough: L is Roman 50; doubled it becomes 100, Roman C.
explanation.definitionFit: Decor is the style of a room's furnishing and decoration.

clue.text: Trotters supported animal home — after altruist, essentially gets out of practice

indicators.note: the animal home comes after the middle letters
essentially means the central letters at the heart of the word

parts.note: a sty is the home of a pig, an animal standing on trotters

explanation.surface: The Trotters back an animal shelter after an altruist loses their touch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trotters' looks like the sitcom family but is pigs' feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Rusty describes skills that have deteriorated from lack of use.

clue.text: Mediocre pencil skirts' material

indicators.note: the phrase skirts round the answer, which lies hidden inside it

explanation.surface: An unremarkable pencil skirt's fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pencil skirts' reads as a garment, but 'skirts'' says the phrase surrounds the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Crepe is a thin fabric with a crinkled surface.

clue.text: It ignites quarrel and Grandad's in bits

parts.note: to spar is to argue or quarrel
split into bits, Grandad becomes grand (K, a thousand) and ad (a plug or advert)

explanation.surface: A row breaks out and Grandad Trotter is in pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: Grandad is the Trotter grandfather, but the word is broken into grand, K for a thousand, and ad, a plug.
explanation.definitionFit: A spark plug fires the fuel mixture in an engine's cylinder.

clue.text: Sparseness of Sun — God, Rodney's gutted about it

parts.note: Ra is the Egyptian sun god

indicators.note: about says the gutted name goes round the it
gutted removes the insides, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: Rodney is Del Boy's younger brother

explanation.surface: Rodney, a reader of the Sun, is devastated about some scarcity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gutted' looks like Rodney's dismay but means emptied, leaving RY.
explanation.definitionFit: Rarity is the quality of being uncommon or scarce.

clue.text: Enthusiasm, journalist for Independent conveyed

indicators.note: for says one piece stands in place of the other

parts.note: passion means intense enthusiasm
ED is an editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A journalist's zeal for the Independent was handed on.
explanation.definitionFit: Passed on means transmitted or handed to someone else.
